rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamazāt are forceful pushing or agitation; Satan's attacks come through whispering and by stirring enemies to harm the Prophet and believers.
rows.anchor: وهو الدفع والتحريك الشديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking God's refuge from Satan keeps a person alert about actions, strengthens obedience, and restrains disobedience.
rows.anchor: داعية إلى التمسك بالطاعة وزاجرا عن المعصية

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan reports the Prophet's prayer after opening prayer: hamz means the madness that seizes a person, nafth is poetry, and nafkh is pride.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن كان عليه السلام يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation asks protection from devils' presence during Quran recitation so the reader remembers and is less forgetful.
rows.anchor: أن يحضرون عند قراءة القرآن لكي يكون متذكرا فيقل سهوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others understand the prayer as seeking protection from the devils' very presence, which prompts their whispering.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون بل استعاذ بالله من نفس حضورهم لأنه الداعي إلى وسوستهم

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet taught a man troubled by insomnia to seek refuge in God's complete words from divine anger, punishment, servants' evil, and devils' promptings and presence.
rows.anchor: روي عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf connects “until” to the earlier description: their bad mention continues until death; the intervening verse emphasizes turning away from them with God's help against Satan.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) حتى متعلق بيصفون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says one who neglected charity and pilgrimage asks to return at death; when challenged that only disbelievers ask, he cites the warning to spend before death.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك كنت جالسا عند ابن عباس

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet says that, as death approaches, a person sees all the rights he had withheld brought before him and asks to return and act righteously.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request is by disbelievers: believers who see their place in Paradise would not wish for more, while the least rewarded would otherwise grieve over higher ranks.
rows.anchor: والأقرب هو الأول إذا عرف المؤمن منزلته في الجنة فإذا شاهدها لا يتمنى أكثر منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited warning to spend before death describes worldly life, not the state of reward, so it does not overturn the preferred reading.
rows.anchor: فهو إخبار عن حال الحياة في الدنيا لا عن حال الثواب فلا يلزم على ما ذكرنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most interpreters place the request at the moment of death's direct apprehension, when the person is compelled to recognize God and his disobedience.
rows.anchor: فالأكثرون على أنه يسأل في حال المعاينة لأنه عندها يضطر إلى معرفة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others place the request when the condemned see Hell in the afterlife, drawing on other descriptions of Hell's inhabitants asking to return.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون بل يقول ذلك عند معاينة النار في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse itself attaches the request to death's arrival, so there is no reason to abandon that apparent timing, even if they later ask again.
rows.anchor: فعلق قولهم هذا بحال حضور الموت وهو حال المعاينة فلا وجه لترك هذا الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the plural “return me” as addressing the angels who seize souls; on this view “Lord” is an oath invoking the Lord's right.
rows.anchor: الملائكة الذين يقبضون الأرواح وهم جماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others take the addressee to be God, with the plural expressing reverence; a poet's plural address illustrates this form.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون بل المراد هو الله تعالى لأن قوله رب بمنزلة أن يقول يا رب

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line supplies an example of plural address used for a singular addressee as a form of reverence.
rows.anchor:
قال الشاعر :
فإن شئت حرمت النساء سواكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person may ask for a return even while knowing it cannot occur; such supplication is permissible, and the wish may be a mere hope.
rows.anchor: فلا يمتنع أن يسألوه لأن الاستعانة بهذا الجنس من المسألة تحسن وإن علم أنه لا يقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Perhaps” does not express doubt: the speaker is resolved to obey if returned, like someone certain he will repair a known failure.
rows.anchor: ليس المراد بلعل الشك فإنه في هذا الوقت باذل للجهد في العزم على الطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, because the future is unknown, people use wording of hope rather than certainty; the Qur'an says returned people would repeat their old conduct.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أيضا أن الأمر المستقبل إذا لم يعرفوه أوردوا الكلام الموضوع للترجي والظن دون اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read “what I left” as the wealth left behind, from which the returned person could pay God's due.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم فيما خلفت من المال ليصير عند الرجعة مؤديا لحق الله تعالى منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others take it more broadly as all neglected duties, bodily and financial worship and rights; this better fits their wish to repair every wrong and disobedience.
rows.anchor: المراد أعمل صالحا فيما قصرت فيدخل فيه العبادات البدنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of “No!” is a refusal of their request, like telling an implausible petitioner “never.” A report to Aisha contrasts the believer's refusal with the disbeliever's request.
rows.anchor: كالجواب لهم في المنع مما طلبوا

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet's report says a believer seeing the angels declines return to worldly grief, while a disbeliever wants it for money, farming, buildings, or waterways; God refuses.
rows.anchor: أنه عليه السلام قال لعائشة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading treats “No!” as confirming that the reported plea really is the word he will utter.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون على وجه الإخبار بأنهم يقولون ذلك وأن هذا الخبر حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers “No!” as a refusal of the requested return.
rows.anchor: والأقرب الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading says the speaker keeps repeating the plea, unable to fall silent under the force of remorse.
rows.anchor: أنه لا يخليها ولا يسكت عنها لاستيلاء الحسرة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another says he alone utters the plea, but it receives no answer and is not heard.
rows.anchor: أنه قائلها وحده ولا يجاب إليها ولا يسمع منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barzakh means a barrier or restraint, as between two seas; death blocks reconciliation and reunion until resurrection, without implying return to worldly life then.
rows.anchor: فالبرزخ هو الحاجز والمانع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of resurrection completely extinguishes hope of return, since the only return then is to the afterlife.
rows.anchor: إنما هو إقناط كلي لما علم أنه لا رجعة يوم البعث إلا إلى الآخرة

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The first and preferred explanation takes the Trumpet as a horn in which a mighty sound is blown, marking the world's destruction and the resurrection; the Prophet calls it a horn.
rows.anchor: روي عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قرن ينفخ فيه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan understands the Trumpet as all forms collectively, with their spirits blown into them; he reads the word with a fatḥa on the wāw.
rows.anchor: أن المراد من الصور مجموع الصور

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: Abu Razin's fatḥa and kasra readings support interpreting the word as the plural of form.
rows.anchor: والفتح والكسر عن أبي رزين وهو حجة لمن فسر الصور بجمع صورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view treats blowing the Trumpet as a metaphor for resurrection and gathering.
rows.anchor: أن النفخ في الصور استعارة والمراد منه البعث والحشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers the literal horn because of the prophetic report; the second blowing also shows that the phrase cannot simply mean the nonrepeating act of enlivening a spirit.
rows.anchor: ليس المراد نفع الروح والإحياء لأن ذلك لا يتكرر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kinship itself remains because the resurrected are the same children and parents; what is denied is the practical effect of kinship.
rows.anchor: فلا يجوز أن يكون المراد نفي النسب في الحقيقة بل المراد نفي حكمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kinship normally brings compassion and mutual appeal, but terror occupies each person with himself and prevents attention to relatives.
rows.anchor: أن يقع به التعاطف والتراحم كما يقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kinship can invite boasting and questions about lineage, but people have no leisure for that in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: أن يحصل به التفاخر في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial can also be a metaphor for extreme fear, when everyone is distracted even from children, siblings, and close kin.
rows.anchor: أن يجعل ذلك استعارة عن الخوف الشديد فكل امرىء مشغول بنفسه عن بنيه وأخيه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that a caller will summon anyone with a claim against a named person; then a woman will rejoice to have a right against even close family.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه يؤخذ العبد والأمة يوم القيامة على رؤوس الأشهاد وينادي مناد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says a person will dread seeing anyone familiar on Judgment Day, fearing that the acquaintance may claim a right against him.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة لا شيء أبغض إلى الإنسان يوم القيامة من أن يرى من يعرفه مخافة أن يثبت له عليه شيء

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: In answer to Aisha, the Prophet says people are distracted from recognition at three scenes: receiving the record, the scales, and the Bridge over Hell.
rows.anchor: عائشة رضي الله عنها يا رسول الله ، أما نتعارف

rows.speaker: الملاحدة
rows.claim: Some object that the denial of questioning and recognition conflicts with verses where people question one another and recognize one another.
rows.anchor: وطعن بعض الملحدة فقال قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fifty-thousand-year Day contains different states: people recognize and question one another at some times and are bewildered at others.
rows.anchor: أن يوم القيامة مقداره خمسون ألف سنة ففيه أزمنة وأحوال مختلفة فيتعارفون ويتساءلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are occupied with themselves after the first blast; after the next blast they turn to each other and ask who raised them from their resting place.
rows.anchor: نفخة واحدة شغلوا بأنفسهم عن التساؤل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They do not ask” can mean that they do not ask about kinship claims.
rows.anchor: المراد لا يتساءلون بحقوق النسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reconciliation takes the statement as describing disbelievers, whose fear is especially severe.
rows.anchor: صفة للكفار وذلك لشدة خوفهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reciprocal questioning described just before belongs to the people of Paradise after they enter it.
rows.anchor: فهو صفة أهل الجنة إذا دخلوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Trumpet comes accounting and the division between the blessed, whose scales are heavy, and the wretched, whose scales are light.
rows.anchor: أن بعد النفخ في الصور تكون المحاسبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some infer that everyone must belong either to the saved or the damned, ruling out people with no entitlement to reward or punishment and those whose two are equal.
rows.anchor: وجب أن يكون كل مكلف لا بد وأن يكون من أهل الجنة وأهل الفلاح أو من أهل النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation treats the scales as a metaphor for justice.
rows.anchor: أحدها : أنه استعارة من العدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second takes the scales as good deeds: deeds with value win, while weightless deeds like a mirage leave their doer in Hell.
rows.anchor: أن الموازين هي الأعمال الحسنة فمن أتي بما له قدر وخطر فهو الفائز الظافر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the scales are plural of weighed things: righteous deeds valued by God; “no weight” means no worth.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما الموازين جمع موزون وهي الموزونات من الأعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation is a real scale with a tongue and two pans, weighing good deeds in beautiful form and evil deeds in ugly form.
rows.anchor: أنه ميزان له لسان وكفتان يوزن فيه الحسنات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains losing oneself as being cheated because the believers inherit the lost person's place.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما غبنوها بأن صارت منازلهم للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the damned cannot benefit from themselves because they are trapped in punishment.
rows.anchor: وقيل امتنع انتفاعهم بأنفسهم لكونهم في العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording that they abide in Hell plainly establishes the unbelievers' everlasting punishment.
rows.anchor: ودلالته على خلود الكفار في النار بينة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf analyzes “abiding in Hell” as an apposition, a second predicate of “those,” or a predicate with an omitted subject.
rows.anchor: بدل من خسروا أنفسهم أو خبر بعد خبر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the fire's striking as hitting and consuming faces' flesh and skin.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أي تضرب وتأكل لحومهم وجلودهم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says lafḥ and nafḥ both mean a blast, but lafḥ has a stronger effect.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : اللفح والنفخ واحد إلا أن اللفح أشد تأثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kāliḥ means the lips retract and pull apart from the teeth, like the heads of roasted animals.
rows.anchor: والكلوح أن تتقلص الشفتان ويتباعدا عن الأسنان

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet describes the upper lip shrinking to the middle of the head and the lower lip drooping to the navel.
rows.anchor: وعن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading has the form “kāliḥūn.”
rows.anchor: وقرىء ( كلحون ) ، ثم إنه سبحانه لما شرح عذابهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condemned are reproached because God's clear signs were recited to them but they denied them, making them deserve the painful punishment.
rows.anchor: فلا جرم صرتم مستحقين لما أنتم فيه من العذاب الأليم

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila argue that the verse assigns punishment to bad deeds, which would be unjust if God created human acts.
rows.anchor: قالت المعتزلة : الآية تدل على أنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi answers that an unmotivated sin would be accidental, not voluntary, and so could not merit punishment; if motivated, its cause was not the person's act without an infinite regress, making the resulting act compelled and undeserving of reward.
rows.anchor: إن صدرت المعصية عنه لا لمرجح ألبتة كان صدورها عنه اتفاقيا لا اختياريا

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Kufan codices read “he said,” referring either to God or the angel ordered to question them; the other regional codices read “say,” referring to an angel or a leader of Hell's inhabitants.
rows.anchor: في مصاحف أهل الكوفة { قال } وهو ضمير الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question is a rebuke: they denied any afterlife and imagined death as lasting extinction, so learning that Hell is eternal makes worldly life look brief and exposes their error.
rows.anchor: فقد كانوا ينكرون اللبث في الآخرة أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may have forgotten the duration amid terrors; their request to ask the counters signals that forgetfulness.
rows.anchor: لعلهم نسوا ذلك لكثرة ما هم فيه من الأهوال وقد اعترفوا بهذا النسيان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says punishment made them forget what happened between the two blasts.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أنساهم ما كانوا فيه من العذاب بين النفختين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, saying “a day or part of a day” minimizes their earthly stay beside the painful punishment they now know.
rows.anchor: تصغير لبثهم وتحقيره بالإضافة إلى ما وقعوا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the question concerns their lifespan in this world: God gave them time to know and act, but they answer that it was short despite having been told the world is brief.
rows.anchor: المراد أنهم أمهلوا حتى تمكنوا من العلم والعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others say it concerns their stay after death; they argue that “in the earth” points to the grave, though the wording can also describe activity in the world.
rows.anchor: بل المراد اللبث في حال الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The after-death view also appeals to criminals swearing they stayed no more than an hour, while believers say they remained until resurrection.
rows.anchor: يقسم المجرمون ما لبثوا غير ساعة

rows.speaker: منكرو عذاب القبر
rows.claim: Those denying grave punishment argue that if the dead were punished in their graves they would know their long stay and would not answer “a day or part of a day.”
rows.anchor: احتج من أنكر عذاب القبر بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question may concern death with no life afterward until resurrection, a period that would include grave punishment.
rows.anchor: لا بد وأن يكون بحسب السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it asks how long they were together, excluding some people's earlier deaths, so their perceived answer can still be a day or part of one.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكونوا سألوا عن قدر اللبث الذي اجتمعوا فيه

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima takes “the counters” to mean the keepers who counted deeds, lifespans, and times of death.
rows.anchor: وهو معنى قول عكرمة فاسأل العادين أي الذين يحسبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation identifies the counters as angels who count the days and hours of worldly life.
rows.anchor: فاسأل الملائكة الذين يعدون أيام الدنيا وساعاتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may instead mean: ask whoever knows the number, since they have forgotten it.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المعنى سل من يعرف عدد ذلك فإنا قد نسيناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A lightened reading, al-ʿādīn, can mean unjust people, who would say the same thing.
rows.anchor: بالتخفيف أي الظلمة فإنهم يقولون مثل ما قلنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading, al-ʿādiyīn, means the long-lived elders, who themselves consider their lives short.
rows.anchor: القدماء المعمرين ، فإنهم يستقصرونها فكيف بمن دونهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their answer is right insofar as earthly life was brief beside the eternal punishment; the point is to show the shortness of worldly days relative to the afterlife.
rows.anchor: فكأنه قيل لهم صدقتم ما لبثتم فيها إلا قليلا إلا أنها انقضت ومضت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “If only you knew” means the stay is brief when one knows of resurrection and gathering; their denial made it seem long.
rows.anchor: قليل لو علمتم البعث والحشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assumption that creation was purposeless and people would not return to God is an even greater reproach.
rows.anchor: أفحسبتم أنما خلقناكم عبثا وأنكم إلينا لا ترجعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do you not see” calls for sight by the mind; izjāʾ means to drive gently and gradually, as in a small consignment and in moving camels at an easy pace.
rows.anchor: والمراد التنبيه والإزجاء السوق قليلا قليلا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says bayna normally takes two or more nouns; the singular pronoun here is explained because cloud is formally singular but collective in meaning.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء ( بين ) لا يصلح إلا مضافا إلى اسمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joining means bringing cloud fragments together into one cloud.
rows.anchor: والتأليف ضم شيء إلى شيء أي يجمع بين قطع السحاب فيجعلها سحابا واحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rukām means gathered or piled, stacking one thing above another until it forms a heap.
rows.anchor: الركم جمعك شيئا فوق شيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses wadq as rain.
rows.anchor: والودق : المطر ، قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses wadq as drops.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد : القطر ، وعن أبي مسلم الأصفهاني

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
rows.claim: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani glosses wadq as water.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي مسلم الأصفهاني : الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khilāl means the cloud's gaps and openings; it is the plural of khalal, like mountains is the plural of mountain.
rows.anchor: من ( شقوقه ومخارقه ) جمع خلل كجبال في جمع جبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reading is reported for the word min at the start of the phrase “from mountains.”
rows.anchor: كجبال في جمع جبل ، وقرىء { من }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cloud formation may mean that God creates clouds successively, or that He transforms other bodies into cloud; on the latter view He creates the qualities that make them clouds.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يغيره من سائر الأجسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then He joins it” implies that cloud parts already existed separately, since joining requires existing things; stacking lets clouds hold much water.
rows.anchor: دلالة على وجودها متقدما متفرقا إذ التأليف لا يصح إلا بين موجودين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cloud formation, rain, snow, hail, dew, and frost are wonders of God's creation and signs of His dominion and power.
rows.anchor: وهذا مما لا بد منه لأن السحاب إنما يحمل الكثير من الماء إذا كان بهذه الصفة

rows.speaker: أهل الطبائع
rows.claim: Natural philosophers say clouds and precipitation usually arise by vapor condensation and less often by air condensation; heat can dissolve small quantities of rising vapor.
rows.anchor: قال أهل الطبائع إن تكون السحاب والمطر والثلج والبرد والطل والصقيع في أكثر الأمر يكون من تكاثف البخار

rows.speaker: أهل الطبائع
rows.claim: When plentiful vapor reaches a cold layer, moderate cold condenses it into cloud and rain; strong cold freezes it into snow before droplets coalesce or hail afterward.
rows.anchor: فإن لم يكن البرد هناك قويا تكاثف ذلك البخار

rows.speaker: أهل الطبائع
rows.claim: Vapor that remains below the cold layer may gather into rain clouds; five causes of that gathering include blocked ascent, pressure by winds or mountains, colliding winds, a slowed heavy leading part, and strong low-level cold.
rows.anchor: أما الأول فذاك لأحد أسباب خمسة

rows.speaker: أهل الطبائع
rows.claim: Low, fine vapor cooled at night condenses into scattered moisture; if it does not freeze it is dew, and if it freezes it is frost, as snow relates to rain.
rows.anchor: فهي قد تنعقد سحابا ماطرا وقد لا تنعقد

rows.speaker: أهل الطبائع
rows.claim: They also explain clouds through contraction of air as it cools.
rows.anchor: فالبخار المجتمع هو السحاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says one cannot assert the natural philosophers' account as necessary, since God may create cloud particles all at once; even if their process occurs, possible bodies still require an efficient cause.
rows.anchor: فعلى الوجه الأول يكون نفس السحاب محدثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every body's particular rising, falling, fineness, density, heat, and cold requires a determiner; if God creates natures and their effects, He is the creator of clouds and rain as well.
rows.anchor: اختصاص كل واحد منها بصفته المعينة من الصعود والهبوط واللطافة والكثافة والحرارة والبرودة لا بد له من مخصص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God creates the natures that move vapor from the earth into the air; when rising vapors accumulate and adhere, He makes them piled clouds, demonstrating His power and wisdom.
rows.anchor: فكان سبحانه هو الذي يزجي سحابا ، لأنه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The majority of commentators, including Mujahid and al-Kalbi, understand the phrase literally: God created mountains of hail in the sky and sends down from them what He wills.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد والكلبي : جبال من برد في السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view calls elevated cloud the sky and compares massive clouds to mountains; hail is frozen water created in cloud, and the cloud may be called mountains because it is made of hail.
rows.anchor: أن السماء هو الغيم المرتفع على رؤوس الناس سمي بذلك لسموه وارتفاعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers literal mountains of hail: “sky” properly names the particular celestial body, while taking it as cloud is figurative; since either is within God's power, the apparent reading should stand.
rows.anchor: والأول أولى لأن السماء اسم لهذا الجسم المخصوص

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi parses the three min particles respectively as marking origin, partitive selection, and explanation of the hail's substance; the object of “sends down” is omitted but understood.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي الفارسي قوله تعالى : { من السماء من جبال فيها من برد } فمن الأولى لابتداء الغاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “strikes by it” refers to hail: it can harm animals and plants, but God sends it where wise and diverts its harm by preventing it from falling elsewhere.
rows.anchor: فالظاهر أنه راجع إلى البرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading hail as stones and their descent as a punishment of annihilation is a remote interpretation.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من حمل البرد على الحجر وجعل نزوله جاريا مجرى عذاب الاستئصال وذلك بعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings include assimilated “sanā barqihi,” a plural barqah for a flash or measure of lightning, and “sanāʾ” with a long vowel; the short form means light and the long form height.
rows.anchor: قرىء { يكاد سنا برقه } على الإدغام

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر المدني
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani reads the bāʾ as extra in “yadhhab bil-abṣār,” with a parallel construction in the prohibition against casting oneself into destruction.
rows.anchor: كقوله : { ولا تلقوا بأيديكم إلى التهلكة } ( البقرة : 195 ) عن أبي جعفر المدني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lightning nearly taking sight must be powerful, pure fire; its appearance from hail, its opposite, demonstrates the work of a wise and capable agent.
rows.anchor: والنار ضد الماء والبرد

rows.speaker: النحويون
rows.claim: Grammarians dispute whether saying “I took Zayd to the house” requires the speaker to go there too; those denying that requirement cite this verse.
rows.anchor: اختلف النحويون في أنك إذا قلت ذهبت بزيد إلى الدار فهل يجب أن تكون ذاهبا معه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's turning of night and day can mean their alternation, one entering into the other, or changes such as cold and heat; all meanings can apply because they bring benefit and reflection.
rows.anchor: وهو كقوله : { وهو الذى جعل اليل والنهار خلفة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding phenomena provide evidence to people of insight and show that people should reflect on them, undermining blind imitation.
rows.anchor: فمن هذا الوجه يدل أن الواجب على المرء أن يتدبر ويتفكر في هذه الأمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about prostrating to what they are ordered can mean prostrating to the one they are ordered to worship, or doing so because of the command.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى للذي تأمرنا بسجوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with yāʾ has them ask one another whether to prostrate to what Muhammad orders, or to the one named al-Raḥmān whose identity they deny.
rows.anchor: وقرىء { * يأمرنا } بالياء كأن بعضهم قال لبعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command should have prompted action and acceptance, yet their aversion increased; their response to the Muslims' prostration explains that reaction.
rows.anchor: وزادهم أمره نفورا ، ومن حقه أن يكون باعثا على الفعل والقبول

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak reports that the Prophet and several Companions prostrated; when the polytheists saw them, they moved away to the side of the mosque in mockery.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك : فسجد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After recounting the disbelievers' aversion to prostration, God recalls signs that reflection on them should reveal the duty to prostrate and worship the Merciful.
rows.anchor: لما حكى عن الكفار مزيد النفرة عن السجود ذكر ما لو تفكروا فيه لعرفوا وجوب السجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burūj are the familiar stations of the planets, named after lofty castles because they are like the planets' dwellings; the word also derives from visible display.
rows.anchor: وأما البروج فهي منازل السيارات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas offers an alternative: the burūj are the great stars.
rows.anchor: وفيه قول آخر عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أن البروج هي الكواكب العظام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers the planetary stations because the pronoun in “in them” most naturally returns to the nearest antecedent, the burūj.
rows.anchor: والأول أولى لقوله تعالى : { وجعل فيها } أي في البروج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lamp is the sun, as another verse calls the sun a lamp.
rows.anchor: والسراج الشمس لقوله تعالى : { وجعل الشمس سراجا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with the plural “lamps” means the sun and the large planets among the stars.
rows.anchor: وقرىء { * سرجا } وهي الشمس والكواكب الكبار فيها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan and al-Aʿmash read the phrase as “a lamp and a luminous moon”; its form can refer to a moonlit night or use the noun moon for moonlight.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والأعمش { سراجا وقمرا منيرا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One meaning of khilfah is that night and day succeed one another, each providing an opportunity to make up work missed in the other.
rows.anchor: أنها عبارة عن كون الشيئين بحيث أحدهما يخلف الآخر ويأتي خلفه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says that an act missed during either night or day can be made up during its counterpart.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما جعل كل واحد منهما يخلف صاحبه فيما يحتاج أن يعمل فيه

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet told Umar to make up missed nighttime voluntary prayer in the day and missed daytime prayer at night.
rows.anchor: قال أنس بن مالك قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لعمر بن الخطاب وقد فاتته قراءة القرآن بالليل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Kisaʾi take khilfah to mean that night and day differ, like black and white or long and short; al-Razi prefers the first view.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مجاهد وقتادة والكسائي يقال لكل شيئين اختلفا هما خلفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi considers the succession-and-compensation interpretation of khilfah more likely.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول أقرب

none: source text is broken; the segment contains only a slash

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion moves from cosmic signs in the winds and clouds to the human being as a sign, tracing life from weakness through strength back to weakness.
rows.anchor: لما أعاد من الدلائل التي مضت دليلا من دلائل الآفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Initial weakness covers fetal life, birth, infancy, nursing, and weaning; strength follows in adulthood, youth, maturity, and full development.
rows.anchor: فقوله من ضعف إشارة إلى حالة كان فيها جنينا وطفلا مولودا ورضيعا ومفطوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After maturity come decline and old age, which is the culmination of weakness.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى ما يكون بعد الكهولة من ظهور النقصان والشيبة هي تمام الضعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He creates what He wills” shows that these stages are due to God's will, paralleling His spreading clouds however He wills.
rows.anchor: إن هذا ليس طبعا بل هو بمشيئة الله تعالى كما قال تعالى في دلائل الآفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge is foregrounded before power here because human development unfolds through stages; in the earlier resurrection passage, power was more prominent because re-creation occurs by command.
rows.anchor: فالقدرة هناك أظهر وههنا المذكور الابداء وهو أطوار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowing and power together warn and promise: God knows people's deeds and conditions, then can reward good and punish evil; knowledge precedes the acts of reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: إذا كان عالما بأعمال الخلق كان عالما بأحوال المخلوقات فإن عملوا خيرا علمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “best of creators” after the account of human creation joins knowledge, which makes creation excellent, with power, expressed by creating.
rows.anchor: في قوله : { فتبارك الله أحسن الخالقين } ( المؤمنون : 14 ) عقيب خلق الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cries do not reduce the punishment: their cries are sounds of the punished, and God does not ease it as an act of grace before they ask; they ask but receive no relief.
rows.anchor: أي لا يخفف وإن اصطرخوا واضطربوا لا يخفف الله من عنده إنعاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their plea to be brought out shows their suffering is punishment, not correction: a pupil who admits wrongdoing would be released, while the punished person is not.
rows.anchor: أن إيلامهم تعذيب لا تأديب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A captive may first hope for release without asking, then ask, and finally promise reform after a long stay when asking alone fails.
rows.anchor: إذا طال لبثه تطلب الإخراج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those lost in this world remain lost in the next, as the verse says whoever is blind here will be blind in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ومن كان فى هاذه أعمى فهو فى الاخرة أعمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They failed to recognize that return to worldly life is distant and impossible according to God's report.
rows.anchor: ثم إنهم لم يعلموا أن العود إلى الدنيا بعيد محال بحكم الإخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their vow to do good is unconditional and omits reliance on God, indicating self-reliance; God replies that sufficient time had been granted for reflection, faith, and action.
rows.anchor: جازمين من غير استعانة بالله ولا مثنوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their promise to do other than what they did exposes the corruption of their former deeds.
rows.anchor: وقولهم : { غير الذي كنا نعمل } إشارة إلى ظهور فساد عملهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers acknowledge that God's grace, not their own knowledge or merit, gave them good; they need forgiveness more than further reward and ask God to act from grace, not strict justice.
rows.anchor: ونحن أحوج إلى تخفيف العذاب منهم إلى تضعيف الثواب فافعل بنا ما أنت أهله نظرا إلى فضلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God guides believers in the afterlife as He guided them in the world; their praise acknowledges their shortcoming and their reception of blessings beyond expectation.
rows.anchor: وكما هدى الله المؤمن في الدنيا هداه في العقبى حتى دعاه بأقرب دعاء إلى الإجابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers say they were settled in the lasting home by God's grace, admitting that their deeds are negligible beside His blessings; the disbelievers instead ask to return and work.
rows.anchor: أي لا عمل لنا بالنسبة إلى نعم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers' promise neglects God's majesty and avoids admitting that they cannot produce deeds proportionate to it; God had supplied both adequate lifespan and a messenger's guidance.
rows.anchor: إغماضا في حق تعظيمه وإعراضا عن الاعتراف بعجزهم عن الإتيان بما يناسب عظمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stated obstacles to belief are either within the people, who failed to reflect on revelation, or in their guide, who failed to recite guidance to them.
rows.anchor: فإن المانع إما أن يكون فيهم حيث لم يتمكنوا من النظر فيما أنزل الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Taste” signals lasting punishment and is a command of humiliation; the wrongdoers have no helper when they need one because they placed words, deeds, and excuses wrongly.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى الدوام وهو أمر إهانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible reading of “no helper” is that a wrongdoer is a person with compounded ignorance, mistaking falsehood for truth, and lacks beneficial knowledge in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: قال بعض الحكماء قوله : { فما للظالمين من نصير } وقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi's preferred broad sense is that no one can help them at all: God will not help, and there is no other helper; proof is called sultan because authority or power aids.
rows.anchor: لأن الله لا ينصره وليس غيره نصيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular “helper” here describes their actual presence in Hell after despairing of human allies and idols, leaving them to hope only for God; elsewhere the warning concerns worldly life or early gathering and expected idol-help.
rows.anchor: أي هذا وقت كونهم واقعين في النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's knowledge of hidden things justifies the unbelievers' lasting punishment: although evil is repaid only in kind, God knows their disbelief is so settled that they would never obey, even if they lived forever.
rows.anchor: وكان يعلم من الكافر أن في قلبه تمكن الكفر بحيث لو دام إلى الأبد لما أطاع الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The contents of the breasts” is apt because the chest is considered through what it contains; its contents are like an occupant or owner, unlike saying a house possesses a person.
rows.anchor: لما كان اعتبار الصدر بما فيه صار ما فيه كالساكن المالك حيث لا يقال الدار ذات زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making people successors cuts off their excuse: they had time and opportunity to know, intellects, messengers who supported reason with transmitted proof, and examples in previous generations whose fate they could see.
rows.anchor: نبهكم بمن مضى وحال من انقضى فإنكم لو لم يحصل لكم علم بأن من كذب الرسل أهلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Successive disbelievers incur greater abhorrence: earlier unbelievers were already hated, those warned by messengers are more culpable, and later people who witness prior punishment yet ignore it are most hated.
rows.anchor: والتالي لهم الذي رأى عذاب من تقدم ولم يخش عذابه أمقت الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelief yields only loss before God and for the unbeliever himself; a lifetime is capital, profitable when spent seeking God's pleasure and lost when spent seeking His displeasure.
rows.anchor: فإن العمر كالرأس مال من اشترى به رضا الله ربح

none: source text is broken; the segment contains only a slash

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Going forward is mentioned before returning because return is easier: it implies that the route was traveled once already, unlike setting out on an unseen route.
rows.anchor: لأن الرجوع أهون من المضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After warning had already cut off one excuse, God answers the claim that more worldly time would have prevented negligence: aging brings increasing weakness, so they wasted the period of ability and would not act in senility either.
rows.anchor: فلو عمرناكم أكثر من ذلك لكان بعده زمان الإزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage follows the claim that God is one and dominant with signs of His power and self-sufficiency, then answers idolaters by describing attributes that constitute divinity.
rows.anchor: فلما بني تلك المسألة على هذه الأصول ذكر عقيبها ما يدل على كمال القدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation of the heavens and earth is an astronomical sign of a powerful God, with fuller proof discussed under another verse.
rows.anchor: وهذا المعنى يدل على وجود الإله القادر من وجوه كثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternation of night and day shows both light and darkness are overcome in turn and therefore subject to a stronger ruler; one grows as the other diminishes.
rows.anchor: وذلك يدل على أن كل واحد منهما مغلوب مقهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takwir means the increasing of one period by the amount the other decreases; a prophetic phrase uses the same root for decline after prosperity.
rows.anchor: والمراد من هذا التكوير أنه يزيد في كل واحد منهما بقدر ما ينقص عن الآخر

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A prophetic supplication seeks refuge from al-ḥawr after al-kawr, meaning reversal or decline after a period of gaining and advancing.
rows.anchor: والمراد من تكوير الليل والنهار ما ورد في الحديث : ( نعوذ الله من الحور بعد الكور )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses describe the same night-day relation as covering, interpenetration, or alternating succession.
rows.anchor: عبر عن هذا المعنى بقوله : { يكور اليل على النهار }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun rules the day and the moon the night, and most benefits of the world depend on them.
rows.anchor: فإن الشمس سلطان النهار والقمر سلطان الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their appointed term is the Day of Resurrection; they continue until then and disappear, as another verse says the sun and moon are joined.
rows.anchor: الأجل المسمى يوم القيامة ، لا يزالان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their subjection means that the celestial spheres move in a fixed orbit until the Resurrection, when the sky will be folded like a scroll.
rows.anchor: أن هذه الأفلاك تدور كدوران المنجنون على حد واحد إلى يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “His is the dominion” is exclusive: if another god had power, the two would conflict, which is impossible; if it had none, it would be deficient, so only God is deity and worthy of worship.
rows.anchor: وهذا يفيد الحصر أي له الملك لا لغيره

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The Sunni argument from “how are you turned away?” is that people were turned from the evidence by an agent other than themselves, namely God; reason supports this because people seek truth but end in error.
rows.anchor: أما أصحابنا فوجه الاستدلال لهم بهذه الآية : أنها صريحة

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila argue that “how are you turned away?” expresses amazement, which would make no sense if God were the one turning them away.
rows.anchor: وأما المعتزلة فوجه الاستدلال لهم : أن قوله : { فأنى تصرفون }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's charge does not seek benefit or avert harm for Him; as the necessary existent in His essence and attributes, He is absolutely self-sufficient.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى ما كلف المكلفين ليجر إلى نفسه منفعة أو ليدفع عن نفسه مضرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God needed something eternally, it would require creation in eternity, a contradiction; if the need arose later, it would be a deficiency no wise being seeks.
rows.anchor: والأول باطل وإلا لزم أن يخلق في الأزل ما كان محتاجا إليه وذلك محال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Regardless of whether appetite or need can be attributed to God, it is necessarily known that the creator of the heavens and all creatures cannot benefit from one person's prayer or be harmed by its absence; all worlds' disbelief cannot harm Him.
rows.anchor: من المعلوم بالضرورة أن الإله القادر على خلق السموات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gains nothing from belief and is harmed by no unbelief, yet He does not approve disbelief.
rows.anchor: يعني أنه وإن كان لا ينفعه إيمان ولا يضره كفران إلا أنه لا يرضى بالكفر

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i argues that if God creates unbelief and whatever He creates is right, He would have approved unbelief in creating it, contrary to this verse.
rows.anchor: احتج الجبائي بهذه الآية من وجهين :

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i also argues that if unbelief were God's decree, believers would have to approve it, but the community agrees that approving unbelief is unbelief; therefore it is neither His decree nor approval.
rows.anchor: لو كان الكفر بقضاء الله تعالى لوجب علينا أن نرضى به لأن الرضا بقضاء الله تعالى واجب

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: One reply says Quranic usage often reserves “His servants” for believers, so the verse means God does not approve unbelief for believers.
rows.anchor: الأصحاب عن هذا الاستدلال من وجوه الأول : أن عادة القرآن

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Another reply distinguishes will from approval: God may will unbelief, while approval means praising and commending an act, as in God's approval of believers.
rows.anchor: أنا نقول الكفر بإرادة الله تعالى ولا نقول إنا برضا الله لأن الرضا عبارة عن المدح عليه

rows.speaker: ضياء الدين عمر
rows.claim: Al-Razi's father Diya al-Din Umar defines approval as refraining from blame or objection, not as will; a verse by Ibn Duraid accepts compulsion while disliking fate.
rows.anchor: الشيخ الوالد ضياء الدين عمر رحمه الله يقول : الرضا عبارة

rows.speaker: ابن دريد
rows.claim: Ibn Duraid's verse says one may accept compulsion while disliking the turns of fate, showing that acceptance and willing are distinct.
rows.anchor: قول ابن دريد : رضيت قسرا وعلى القسر رضا

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: A final reply grants for argument that approval means will, but restricts the verse's general wording by verses where God wills the disbeliever's unbelief.
rows.anchor: والرابع : هب أن الرضا هو الإرادة إلا أن قوله : { ولا يرضى لعباده الكفر } عام
